text.en: Look at your school bag. The bag is cloth, the zip is metal, the bottle is plastic and the pencil is wood. Why are different materials used for different things?

Everything around us is made of materials. An object can be made of one or many materials. Materials may come from nature, like wood and cotton, or be made by people, like plastic.
We group materials by their properties, such as hardness, shine, transparency, and whether they float or dissolve in water. Rough or smooth, hard or soft, light or heavy are also properties.
Metals are usually hard and shiny, and they conduct heat and electricity. Transparent materials such as clear glass let us see clearly through them. Translucent materials let light through but blur details. Opaque materials, such as a wooden board, block the light so we cannot see through them. Some solids dissolve in water, like salt and sugar, and some do not, like sand and chalk. Some materials float on water and some sink, depending on how heavy they are for their size.
Anything that has mass and takes up space is matter. Air is matter even though we cannot see it. Like other matter, it has mass and takes up space. Solid, liquid and gas are three common states of matter.
We choose a material because its properties suit the use. Cooking pans are metal because metal conducts heat. Handles are plastic or wood because they do not conduct heat well.

board.text: Choosing materials

text.en: Imagine a wooden ruler and a wooden spoon. One helps you measure and the other helps you stir. The objects have different shapes and uses, but the same material can make both.

board.text: Ruler and spoon: different objects, same material

text.en: Now imagine a bottle with a steel body and a plastic cap. The body holds water, and the cap closes the opening. A single object can combine materials for different jobs.

board.text: One bottle, more than one material

text.en: Compare a piece of cloth, a thin card and a wooden ruler without breaking them. Gently try to bend them and record how each sample behaves. The cloth may bend more easily than the ruler.

board.text: Property to compare: how easily it bends

text.en: You can group the same samples using another rule, such as how smooth they feel. A sample can be smooth and hard at the same time. Different properties answer different questions.

board.text: One material can have several properties

text.en: A shiny surface might be metal, plastic or another material. Compare a shiny plastic button with a dull metal key. Shine gives us a clue, but it does not identify the material on its own.

board.text: Shine alone does not identify a material

text.en: Place a card with a large letter behind three samples, one at a time. Try clear plastic, tracing paper and thick cardboard. Keep the letter and the light in the same places.

board.text: Same letter and light for all three samples

text.en: The letter is clear through the clear plastic. The tracing paper lets light through, but the letter looks blurred. These observations help us distinguish transparent from translucent.

board.text: Clear plastic: letter is clear
Tracing paper: letter is blurred

text.en: The thick cardboard blocks the view of the letter. It is opaque. A translucent panel works for a softly lit shade, while clear material works when you need to see details.

board.text: Cardboard blocks the view
Choose for the job the material needs to do

text.en: Put equal amounts of room-temperature water in two cups. Stir a little salt into one and a little clean sand into the other. Watch what happens to the grains. Leave both samples untasted.

board.text: Compare salt and sand in water

text.en: The small amount of salt dissolves, so you can no longer see separate grains. The sand grains remain visible and can settle. A change in appearance can help you tell the samples apart.

board.text: Salt: grains no longer visible
Sand: visible grains settle

text.en: Imagine letting the salt water dry slowly in a shallow dish. Solid salt can be left behind. That helps show the dissolved salt was still in the clear water.

board.text: After water evaporates, salt can remain

text.en: An object’s shape also matters when we ask whether it floats. A solid lump of modelling clay may sink. A wide, hollow bowl made from the same lump may float if water stays out of it.

board.text: Same clay, different shape

text.en: The bowl can push more water aside before it is covered. That helps explain how a boat made with a material like steel can float, even though a solid piece of that material sinks.

board.text: A hollow shape can push more water aside

text.en: Put dry tissue inside a clear plastic cup. Turn the cup upside down and lower it straight into a small basin of water. Keep it upright as you lift it out again.

board.text: Cup upside down: air trapped inside

text.en: The tissue can stay dry because the air inside the cup occupies space. Water cannot fill the cup while that space is still occupied by the trapped air.

board.text: Air occupies space even when invisible

text.en: Try tilting the submerged cup so some air escapes as bubbles. Water can move into the space the air leaves. The change shows that there was something inside the cup all along.

board.text: Air leaves as bubbles, water enters

text.en: A window and a covered storage box need different properties. The window needs a material you can see through. The box may need to hide what is inside and be strong enough to hold it.

board.text: Different jobs need different properties

text.en: Pick an object near you. Name a material it is made of, one useful property and one reason a different material might be a poor choice for the same job.

board.text: Object → material → property → purpose

problem.en: Why is clear glass useful in some windows?

text.en: Clear glass is transparent.
So we can see through and let light in.

prompt.en: Explain why a pan has a plastic handle.

requiredIdeas.en: A suitable handle conducts heat less readily than the metal pan.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all shiny things are metal.

points.en: Transparent, translucent and opaque describe light passing.
Matter has mass and takes up space.
The choice of material depends on its use.
